title: How can you learn to speak more clearly in a case interview?
description: The interviewer needs to follow your reasoning. Calm, understandable explanations are more valuable than impressive-sounding language.
hook: You do not need to sound like a consultant to pass a case. You need to be easy to follow. Here are short daily exercises that make a real difference.
body:
Why this matters

The interviewer needs to follow your reasoning. Calm, understandable explanations are more valuable than impressive-sounding language.

Three exercises (5 to 10 minutes a day)

Warm up your speech

Use SpeechOn.app (free) for a short guided warm-up. Relax your jaw, practise articulation and read a few business sentences aloud.

Give a 60-second recommendation

Answer first, explain two reasons, mention a risk and finish with a next step. Record yourself and listen for confusing sentences.

Replace rush with pauses

Practise saying a sentence, pausing briefly, and continuing. It is fine to take thinking time. Aim for clarity rather than sounding unusually formal.

Keep it small

Short and regular beats long and occasional. Ten minutes most days will do more than two hours on a Sunday. Tick it off and move on with your day.

Practise the handoff between thinking and speaking

Choose one simple business calculation and explain it aloud in three parts: the equation, the result and the meaning. For example: "Revenue is 10,000 orders multiplied by £40 per order, so £400,000. Because orders are unchanged, any revenue decline would have to come from order value." That is a complete, understandable thought.

Record your explanation once. Listen for sentences that change direction halfway through, unsupported claims and numbers without units. Then record it again with a short pause between the calculation and the implication. You do not need a particular accent or a performative executive voice.

Speech warm-ups may help you feel ready to speak, but they do not replace practice on case-specific explanations. Use them as preparation, not as a substitute for reasoning.
outro: All three routines, with links to free tools, are on the interview skills page. Next in this topic: How do you build business judgement if you are new to business?
